title: Uterine Rupture in Pregnancy
article_subtype: Clinical review incorporating a literature search and pooled analyses
clinical_background: Uterine rupture is uncommon but can cause severe maternal and fetal harm. It involves disruption through the full thickness of the uterine wall and its overlying serosa, and can occur in an unscarred uterus or one with a surgical scar. Uterine scar dehiscence differs because the serosa remains intact and major maternal or fetal complications are uncommon. Early manifestations of rupture are often nonspecific, making diagnosis difficult; after diagnosis, delivery generally needs to occur within 10-37 minutes to avert clinically significant fetal morbidity. Previous uterine surgery and several obstetric factors increase risk, although rupture remains infrequent even in higher-risk groups.
study_design: Literature review with pooled analysis of observational studies and reviews. The authors searched PubMed, Medline, and Cochrane for relevant English-language publications and also traced references. The search covered articles published from 1976 through May, 2012.

population.description: Pregnant women represented in the included publications. The analysis of uterine rupture incidence across 25 studies comprised 2,951,297 pregnant women.
inclusion_criteria: English-language, peer-reviewed articles published from 1976 through May, 2012 that reported uterine rupture incidence and provided sufficient detail about the authors’ definitions of uterine rupture and uterine scar dehiscence

comparators: Incidence across patient subgroups defined by uterine scar status and other risk factors
Incidence in women with unscarred uteri in industrialized versus developing countries

primary: Incidence of uterine rupture during pregnancy

statistical_methods: The authors pooled incidence data from 25 studies and examined a subset of 8 studies reporting spontaneous rupture of unscarred uteri in developed countries. They also compared reported rates across patient subgroups; no formal statistical model for their pooled analysis is specified.
interpretation: The article characterizes pregnancy-related uterine rupture as uncommon but potentially catastrophic. It gives an overall incidence of 0.07% and identifies women with a normal, unscarred uterus in industrialized countries as the lowest-risk group, at 1 in 8,434 pregnancies (0.012%). Most ruptures occur in scarred uteri, particularly after cesarean delivery. Risk varies with the type and number of uterine scars, previous vaginal birth, interpregnancy interval, uterine anatomy, fetal size, and labor management. A sustained, marked fetal bradycardia is the most dependable early warning sign; abdominal pain, abnormal labor progress, and vaginal bleeding are less consistent. Prompt delivery is critical, although intervention within 10-37 minutes cannot always prevent severe fetal injury.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The authors contrast their assessment with earlier reports that may have classified asymptomatic scar dehiscence as complete rupture, potentially explaining higher historical estimates for classic cesarean scars. Findings on oxytocin augmentation after cesarean delivery conflict: some cited studies suggest increased rupture risk, whereas others found no significant association. Studies of gestation beyond 40 weeks likewise disagree about whether rupture risk rises. Evidence on single-layer hysterotomy closure is mixed, although several cited analyses associate it with greater risk. Earlier literature reported higher perinatal mortality after rupture than more recent studies. Reported maternal mortality is also substantially higher in developing than in developed countries.
clinical_implications: A prior cesarean scar carries a rupture risk even without a subsequent trial of labor; risks observed during TOLAC should be interpreted against that baseline.
Uterine scar dehiscence and complete rupture have different clinical consequences and management options and must not be treated as equivalent findings.

Fetal compromise can develop rapidly after rupture, especially when the fetus or placenta enters the abdominal cavity. The general 20-30-minute target for starting cesarean delivery after a diagnosis of fetal distress offers limited protection against permanent fetal injury in that circumstance.

Fetal heart-rate abnormalities are more useful for recognizing rupture than maternal abdominal pain or changes in measured uterine activity. Epidural anesthesia has not been reported to delay diagnosis of rupture.

The article identifies subgroups whose rupture risk exceeds its illustrative threshold of 1 in 200 women (0.5%), including women with multiple cesarean scars, certain prior uterine incisions or closures, a short interdelivery interval, prior myomectomy, and selected circumstances involving induction, augmentation, or fetal macrosomia.

The time available to prevent major maternal harm may be longer than the fetal interval when fluid resuscitation and blood transfusion are available, but uterine hemorrhage can still be life-threatening.
practice_implications: When rupture is suspected, maintain a high level of suspicion, rapidly mobilize available resources, stabilize the mother, and proceed promptly to delivery and definitive surgical treatment.

After delivery, select maternal surgery according to the rupture's type and extent, hemorrhage, the mother's condition, and her wishes about future childbearing. Reserve uterine repair for the circumstances specified in the article, including a low transverse rupture, controllable bleeding, good general condition, and no evidence of evolving coagulopathy. Consider hysterectomy the treatment of choice for intractable bleeding or multiple, longitudinal, or low-lying rupture sites.

For patients in a subgroup exceeding the article's illustrative risk threshold of 1 in 200 women (0.5%), develop an individualized management plan that takes the increased risk into account; the article describes the choice of a tolerable threshold as inherently dependent on patient, clinician, and societal risk tolerance.
Carefully consider labor induction in women with congenital uterine anomalies, particularly when they have also had a cesarean delivery.

The cited ACOG guidance discourages prostaglandins for labor induction in most women with a previous cesarean delivery because of evidence of increased rupture risk. The authors advise judicious oxytocin use and monitoring during VBAC trials and report the cited investigators' suggested upper limit of 20 mU/min.
The authors present induction using a transcervical Foley catheter alone as a potentially reasonable option for a woman undergoing TOLAC with an unfavorable cervix.

The cited ACOG guidance advises against restricting access to VBAC generally. It also states that suspected fetal macrosomia or gestation beyond 40 weeks alone should not rule out TOLAC, that eligible women with twin gestations and one previous low transverse cesarean incision may be considered for TOLAC, and that women with two previous low transverse cesarean deliveries may be considered regardless of previous vaginal delivery.
The cited ACOG guidance finds no absolute contraindication to epidural anesthesia during TOLAC. The cited investigators recommend avoiding single-layer closure in women contemplating a future VBAC.
limitations: No accurate model is available to predict an individual's risk of uterine rupture.

Studies of oxytocin often fail to distinguish labor augmentation from induction, despite differences in patient characteristics and typical dosing. Available data on augmentation versus induction are sparse and conflicting, and observational comparisons generally lack adequate adjustment for confounding by indication.
The increased rupture risk attributable to oxytocin in women with unscarred uteri remains uncertain because the available information is limited.

Reports following myomectomy often omit operative features needed to assess subsequent rupture risk, including the number and location of incisions, entry into the uterine cavity, and closure technique. In several laparoscopic-myomectomy studies, few patients labored and scheduled cesarean delivery was common.
Evidence concerning rupture risk for an unknown uterine scar includes studies that the article describes as substantially underpowered.

The cited prostaglandin-induction study reporting no ruptures was underpowered to detect small differences. Evidence on mechanical cervical-ripening methods is limited, and concomitant oxytocin complicates interpretation of the cited Foley-catheter findings.
Comparisons involving low vertical cesarean scars are hampered by inconsistent definitions of when an incision extends sufficiently into the upper uterine segment to be considered classic.
The cited small studies associating advanced gestation with rupture may differ from larger studies because of sample size or uncertainty in gestational-age assessment.

Evidence for IUPC monitoring during VBAC trials is insufficient to establish a morbidity or mortality benefit. Studies of proposed diagnostic imaging methods are limited by retrospective design and lack of surgical confirmation of true dehiscence; CT and MRI have limited usefulness for acute diagnosis because of time constraints.
open_questions: The precise increase in rupture risk associated with each type of congenital uterine malformation remains uncertain.
Whether ruptures occurring away from a previous laparoscopic-myomectomy scar were attributable to the earlier myomectomy remains unresolved.
The benefit of IUPC monitoring of contractions during VBAC trials remains unclear.
future_directions: The authors call for further study of how myomectomy characteristics affect rupture risk in later pregnancies.
They also state that investigations after laparoscopic myomectomy need long-term follow-up, given reports of rupture years after surgery.

main_conclusion: The authors conclude that uterine rupture is uncommon but can rapidly cause severe fetal and maternal harm, particularly in pregnancies with a uterine scar. Persistent, profound fetal bradycardia is the most dependable early warning sign; prompt operative delivery is critical, although even intervention within 10-37 minutes cannot invariably prevent serious neonatal injury.
narrative_summary: This review examined English-language observational studies and reviews of uterine rupture, using PubMed, Medline, Cochrane and reference tracing; 133 articles were included for extraction and analysis. The authors distinguish full-thickness rupture, which involves the uterine serosa and can cause major hemorrhage and fetal compromise, from scar dehiscence, which generally has less serious consequences. Rupture is rare in an unscarred uterus in industrialized countries: the text reports 1 in 8,434 pregnancies (0.012%). Prior cesarean delivery accounts for most cases. Risk varies with scar type and number, previous vaginal birth, interdelivery interval, uterine anomaly, fetal size, and induction or augmentation. Evidence about some associations, including oxytocin use during augmentation and pregnancy beyond 40 weeks, is conflicting or limited. Prolonged fetal-heart-rate deceleration or bradycardia is more consistent than abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding or altered uterine contractions as an early indicator. Once rupture is suspected, the review emphasizes rapid mobilization for maternal stabilization and operative delivery: the reported interval before major fetal morbidity is only 10-37 minutes, and rapid delivery does not always avert neonatal injury. Following delivery, uterine repair is reserved for selected stable patients with controllable bleeding who desire future childbearing; hysterectomy is the preferred treatment for intractable bleeding or multiple, longitudinal or low-lying rupture sites. subgroup_analyses: Gardeil et al observed unscarred rupture in 1 per 30,764 deliveries (0.0033%): no cases among 21,998 primigravidas and 2 (0.0051%) among 39,529 multigravidas without a uterine scar.

An analysis of 8 studies dated 1975-2009 identified 174 ruptures among 1,467,534 deliveries in industrialized countries, reported in the prose as 0.012% (1 in 8,434). The article states that most spontaneous unscarred ruptures occurred at term during labor.

Parity findings from cited studies differed: Golan et al recorded parity greater than 5 in 19 of 61 rupture cases (31%); Schrinsky and Benson recorded parity greater than 4 in 7 of 22 unscarred-rupture cases (32%); Mokgokong and Marivate reported mean parity 4; Gardeil et al reported rupture in 2 of 39,529 multigravidas without a previous scar (0.005%).

Of 22 unscarred ruptures reported by Schrinsky and Benson, 19 occurred during labor (86%) and 3 before labor (14%); the article describes the timing among women with previous scars as nearly evenly divided.

Oxytocin exposure among unscarred-rupture cases was reported as 32 of 260 (12%) by Mokgokong and Marivate, 9 of 65 (14%) by Rahman et al, and 26 of 61 (43%) by Golan et al; Plauche et al attributed 1 of 23 (4%) to oxytocin. The article considers the attributable increase in risk uncertain.

Ravasia et al observed rupture during attempted VBAC in 8% (2 of 25) of women with congenitally malformed uteri versus 0.61% (11 of 1,788) with normal uteri (P =.013); both anomaly-group ruptures followed induction with prostaglandin E2.

A separate study reported no ruptures among 165 patients with Müllerian duct anomalies who entered spontaneous labor after 1 previous cesarean. The anomaly categories were minor in 36% (60 of 165) and major in 64% (105 of 165); 6% (10 of 165) underwent induction.

For pregnancy implanted in a rudimentary uterine horn, the article associates induction with rupture in ≤ 81% (387 of 475 cases). Of ruptures in these pregnancies, 80% occurred before the third trimester and 67% during the second trimester.

After transabdominal myomectomy, Brown et al reported no ruptures among pregnancies yielding 120 term infants, with 80% delivered vaginally; Garnet reported 3 ruptures among 83 women (4%) undergoing elective cesarean because of a previous myomectomy.

Dubuisson et al observed 3 ruptures in subsequent pregnancies among 100 women with previous laparoscopic myomectomy. Only 1 was at the operative scar, yielding the authors' attributed risk estimate of 1% (95% CI, 0-5.5%); attributing the other 2 to myomectomy would produce 3%, but the article questions that attribution.

Four other laparoscopic-myomectomy studies found no ruptures among 320 pregnancies; scheduled cesarean proportions were 80%, 79%, 75%, and 65%, respectively. A Japanese prospective study reported none among 59 successful vaginal births, while an Italian multicenter study recorded 1 spontaneous rupture at 33 weeks' gestation among 386 pregnancies (0.26%).

For a classic vertical cesarean scar, Rosen et al reported rupture in 3 of 26 unplanned TOLAC cases (11.5%). Chauhan et al reported 0.64% (95% CI, 0.13.5%) among 157 women undergoing repeat cesarean, of whom 49% were in labor at delivery; the confidence interval is printed as shown.

Landon et al reported rupture in 2 of 105 women (1.9%) with a previous classic, inverted T, or J incision who presented in advanced labor or declined repeat cesarean. Chauhan et al separately found asymptomatic scar dehiscence in 9% (95% CI, 5-15%), which the article contrasts with historically reported rupture rates of 4-9%.

A meta-analysis of 5 studies found symptomatic rupture in 12 of 1,112 TOLAC cases (1.1%) with a low vertical scar; the article reports no significantly greater rupture risk or adverse maternal and perinatal outcomes than with low transverse scars. Naef et al reported 0.62% across 322 later pregnancies: 1.15% among 174 TOLAC patients and no ruptures among 148 elective repeat-cesarean patients.

For an unknown cesarean scar, the MFMU Network registry reported rupture in 15 of 3,206 TOLAC patients (0.5%). The cited 70-patient case-control study and 2 additional case series did not identify an association or materially different rates, but the article describes them as underpowered.

In the Grubb et al randomized trial involving 1 or 2 unknown previous incisions, oxytocin augmentation (n=95) versus no intervention (n=93) yielded 4 dehiscences and 1 rupture, all in the augmented group. The rupture occurred in a patient with 2 previous cesareans, including one vertical incision.
Ravasia et al reported 0.45% rupture among 1,544 patients laboring spontaneously after previous cesarean; Zelop et al reported 0.72% among 2,214 women with 1 previous cesarean laboring spontaneously.

For oxytocin during TOLAC, Cahill et al gave attributable rupture risks of 2.9% and 3.6% at maximum dose ranges of more than 20 mU/min and more than 30 mU/min, respectively. The article also cites an earlier meta-analysis and Zelop et al as finding no significant increased rupture association with oxytocin; it cautions against treating unadjusted observational comparisons as decisive.

Bujold et al found no statistically significant difference among rupture rates with spontaneous labor (1.1%), induction by amniotomy with or without oxytocin (1.2%), and induction using a transcervical Foley catheter (1.6%; P =0.81). Hoffman et al instead reported a 3.67-fold increased risk (95% CI, 1.46-9.23) with a Foley catheter for cervical ripening; many patients also received oxytocin.

Pettker et al found that adding oxytocin to a transcervical Foley catheter did not shorten time to delivery or change delivery within 24 hours or vaginal-delivery rate; no numerical effect estimate is supplied. A systematic review comparing induction (4,038 women) with spontaneous labor (13,374 women) after previous cesarean reported fewer vaginal births and more rupture/dehiscence, repeat cesarean delivery, and postpartum hemorrhage with induction; hysterectomy and neonatal outcomes were similar.

Landon et al reported no ruptures among 227 patients induced with prostaglandins alone; the study was underpowered for small differences. Exposures were misoprostol in 52, dinoprostone in 111, PGE2 gel in 60, and combined prostaglandins in 4; no significant effect of prostaglandin type was apparent.

In the MFMU Network study of 11,778 women, induction versus spontaneous TOLAC was associated with more rupture among those without previous vaginal delivery (1.5% vs 0.8%, P =0.02). Among those with previous vaginal delivery, the comparison of spontaneous TOLAC with induction was not significant (0.6% vs 0.4%, P =0.42).

Esposito et al reported mean interpregnancy intervals of 20.4 ± 15.4 months among 23 rupture cases after previous cesarean versus 36.5 ± 30.4 months in controls (P =.01). Bujold et al reported rupture in 2.8% with interdelivery interval ≤24 months versus 0.9% with >24 months (P< .01) among 1,527 TOL patients; adjusted OR 2.65 (95% CI, 1.08-5.46).

The article reports a rupture rate of 5.6% when an interdelivery interval of ≤24 months coincided with single-layer hysterotomy closure; its proposed explanation involving scar tensile strength is presented as speculation.
Durnwald and Mercer did not find increased rupture among 182 women with single-layer closure, but reported more uterine windows than after multilayer closure: 3.5% versus 0.7% (P =.046).

Across 10 studies dated 1993-2010, subsequent-pregnancy rupture after 2 or more cesareans ranged from 0.9-6.0% (1 per 17-108 pregnancies), described as 2- to 16-fold higher than after a single cesarean. The cited studies' different estimates and the nonsignificant MFMU comparison are retained separately in main_findings.

Fox reviewed 37 women (59 pregnancies) with previous rupture and 50 women (75 pregnancies) with previous dehiscence; rupture occurred in one pregnancy (0.7% of pregnancies; 1.2% of women), with no deaths.
For twin versus singleton pregnancies undergoing VBAC, Ford et al reported rupture rates of 0.9% versus 0.8% among 1,850 twin-gestation patients and the singleton comparison group.

Cahill et al compared 535 twin with 24,307 singleton pregnancies during TOLAC after at least 1 previous cesarean: rupture rates were 1.1% versus 0.9% (OR, 1.2; 95% CI, 0.3-4.6). The twin group was less likely to attempt TOLAC (OR, 0.3; 95% CI 0.2-.04), without greater VBAC failure (OR, 1.1; 95% CI, 0.8-1.6) or major maternal morbidity (OR, 1.6; 95% CI, 0.7-3.7).

Varner et al reported rupture at 0.7% in both multifetal (4/556) and singleton (99/13,923) TOLAC groups after one previous cesarean [ORadj 1.19 (0.43-3.30)]. Aaronson et al reported no rupture among 134 twin pregnancies undergoing TOLAC after a single cesarean.

Among women with 1 previous cesarean and no previous vaginal delivery, Elkousy et al reported rupture of 3.6% with fetal weight more than 4000 g versus the group weighing < 4000 g (RR 2.3, P< .001); the article does not give the latter group's absolute rate in this comparison. Flamm et al reported no rate difference by neonatal weight ≥4000 gm versus < 4000 gm in a cohort of 301 women.

At later gestation, Hammoud et al also reported lower odds of successful vaginal delivery at ≥41 weeks than at 37-40 6/7 weeks (OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.51–0.89). Zelop et al found no significant rupture-rate difference for TOLAC at more than 40 weeks versus 37-40 weeks: 1.3% (17 of 1,271) versus 0.8% (12 of 1,504), P = 0.2.

Zelop et al reported rupture with spontaneous labor in 0.5% at or before 40 weeks versus 1.0% after 40 weeks (P = 0.2); with induced labor, corresponding rates were 2.1% and 2.6% (P = 0.7). They attributed the increased risk to induction regardless of gestational age rather than a substantial increase after 40 weeks.

Bujold and Gauthier found abnormal fetal-heart-rate patterns to be the first manifestation in 87% of rupture cases. Leung et al found prolonged deceleration in 79% of cases, and Rodriguez et al reported fetal distress in 78%. The article states that prolonged deceleration invariably accompanied extrusion of the placenta and fetus into the abdomen in the cited cases.

Across 9 studies dated 1980-2002, abdominal pain occurred in 13-60% of rupture cases. Among 10,967 TOLAC patients in a cited review, 22% of complete ruptures presented with abdominal pain and 76% with fetal-distress signs on continuous monitoring. Bujold and Gauthier identified pain as the first sign in 5% of patients.

Rodriguez et al observed none of the classically described reductions in uterine tone or activity among 76 rupture cases, including 39 monitored with IUPCs; fetal and maternal morbidity and mortality did not differ between IUPC use and external tocodynamometry in that study. Across 8 reports dated 1980-2002, vaginal bleeding occurred in 11-67% of rupture cases; across 3 studies, hypovolemic shock occurred in 29-46%.

For prediction after cesarean, Rozenberg et al studied 642 women at 36-38 weeks and found significantly increased rupture risk when the lower uterine segment measured less than 3.5 mm. At a 3.5 mm cutoff, sensitivity was 88%, specificity 73.2%, positive predictive value 11.8%, and negative predictive value 99.3%. Gotoh et al studied 722 women within 1 week of delivery and reported significantly increased risk with a wall thinner than 2 mm; positive and negative predictive values were 73.9% and 100%.

Table 3 reports fetal or neonatal hypoxia or anoxia in 19 of 231 rupture cases (8%); acidosis defined by umbilical artery cord pH < 7 in 83 of 252 (33%); five-minute Apgar score < 7 in 90 of 349 (26%); and neonatal intensive care admission in 71 of 164 (43%).

Table 3 reports perinatal death in 39 of 548 rupture cases (7%) in industrialized countries versus 388 of 524 (74%) in developing countries. For maternal consequences, it reports severe blood loss or transfusion in 67 of 286 (23%), cystotomy in 45 of 311 (11%), need for hysterectomy in 109 of 518 (21%), death in 1 of 313 (0.32%) in industrialized countries, and death in 41 of 524 (8%) in developing countries.

Leung et al observed neonatal asphyxia in 5 of 99 neonates (5%) after maternal rupture. None had clinically significant perinatal morbidity when delivery occurred within 17 minutes of an isolated prolonged fetal-heart-rate deceleration; when severe late decelerations preceded it, asphyxia occurred as soon as 10 minutes after onset of the prolonged deceleration.

Menihan reported bradycardia 18-37 minutes before delivery in 6 of 11 fetuses after rupture. Fetal acidosis occurred in 91%, without permanent neurologic injury or neonatal death in that study. Bujold and Gauthier observed hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy with impaired motor development in 2 neonates despite intervention within < 18-min among 23 rupture cases.

Among 99 rupture cases, Leung et al found umbilical-artery pH less than 7 in 43 newborns (43%), including 25 with pH less than 6.8; 39 newborns (39%) had a 5-minute Apgar score less than 7, including 12 with a score less than 3. Menihan found cord pH less than 7.0 in 10 of 11 fetuses (91%) and a 5-minute Apgar score less than 7 in 5 (45%); complete fetal and placental extrusion was the principal factor associated with fetal acidosis.
Neonatal intensive care admission after rupture was reported by Menihan in 8 of 11 newborns (73%), Kieser and Baskett in 8 of 18 (45%), and Landon et al in 46 of 144 (32%).

A historical review by Schrinsky and Benson identified 620 infant deaths among 960 rupture cases across 33 studies, for perinatal mortality of 65%. More recent cited estimates include Blanchette et al, 2 deaths (17%) among 12 rupture cases; Leung et al, 6 deaths (6%) among 99; Lydon-Rochelle et al, 5.5% among fetuses in 91 rupture cases versus 0.5% in controls; and Landon et al, 2% (2 of 124).

For maternal blood loss after rupture, Cowan et al reported mean loss of 1,500 mL among 5 patients, symptomatic in 3 (60%). Transfusion was reported by Shipp et al in 25% (7 of 28), Kieser and Baskett in 44% (8 of 18), and Leung et al in 29% (29 of 99).
Hypovolemic shock after rupture was reported by Golan et al in 29% of 93 cases and Rahman et al in 33 of 96 (34%); Eden et al reported 46% (11 of 24 cases) in an earlier literature review.

Bladder injury after rupture was reported by Lydon-Rochelle et al in 8% (7 of 91) versus 1.2% (240 of 20,004) of controls without rupture (P =.001); Shipp et al reported 18% (5 of 28), and Kieser and Baskett reported cystotomy in 17% (3 of 18). Leung et al reported incidental cystotomy in 12% (12 of 99) plus ruptured bladder or accidental cystotomy in 7 more (7%), for a combined urologic injury rate of 19%.

Hysterectomy after rupture was reported in 78% (261 of 335) in a South African study, 8% (3 of 39) by Flamm et al, 6% (1 of 18) by Kieser and Baskett, 17% (2 of 12) by Blanchette et al, 60% (6 of 10) by Hibbard et al, and 19% (19 of 99) by Leung et al. In the last study, indications among the hysterectomies included an unrepairable uterus in 13 (68%), intractable atony in 4 (21%), and placenta accreta in 1 (5%).

The article reports maternal mortality after rupture of 0-1% in modern developed nations versus 5-10% in developing countries. In a South African study, 22 of 260 women with rupture of an unscarred uterus died (8.5%); mortality by tear type was 15 of 183 (8.2%) for longitudinal, 2 of 49 (4%) for transverse, 2 of 16 (13%) for posterior-wall, and 3 of 12 (25%) for multiple tears.

Golan et al reported no maternal deaths among 32 women with rupture of a scarred uterus versus 9 deaths among 61 with an intact uterus (15%). Leung et al reported 1 death (1%) among 99 rupture patients. Mokgokong and Marivate reported maternal mortality of 4.5% when rupture was diagnosed before delivery versus 10.4% when diagnosed afterward.

document_sections.heading: Overview
document_sections.content: Uterine rupture in pregnancy is uncommon but often catastrophic, with substantial fetal and maternal morbidity. Numerous factors raise risk, although rupture remains uncommon even in high-risk groups. Publications from 1976-2012 described 2,084 ruptures among 2,951,297 pregnant women across 25 reports, giving an overall rate of 1 in 1,146 pregnancies (0.07%). Early manifestations are usually nonspecific, complicating diagnosis and sometimes delaying treatment. The interval from diagnosis to delivery is generally only 10-37 minutes before clinically important fetal injury becomes inevitable; catastrophic bleeding, fetal anoxia, or both cause that injury. Warning findings vary, and the brief opportunity for definitive treatment makes rupture particularly concerning to clinicians.

document_sections.heading: Definition
document_sections.content: Rupture can affect an unscarred uterus or one with a prior surgical scar. It entails disruption through the entire uterine wall and its covering visceral peritoneum, or uterine serosa, and is associated with clinically important uterine bleeding, fetal distress, fetal and/or placental passage into the abdomen, urgent cesarean delivery, and uterine repair or hysterectomy. Uterine scar dehiscence instead separates an existing scar. It is more common and seldom causes major maternal or fetal complications: the peritoneum stays intact, substantial bleeding from the scar edges does not occur, and the fetus, placenta, and cord remain inside the uterine cavity. Any cesarean delivery in dehiscence is undertaken for another obstetric indication, not fetal distress caused by the defect. Although previous surgery, especially cesarean delivery, raises rupture risk, most scar disruptions are dehiscences. Distinguishing the conditions matters because management options and outcomes differ substantially.

document_sections.heading: Sources of information and study selection
document_sections.content: The review searched PubMed, Medline, and Cochrane for pertinent English-language peer-reviewed literature, using uterine rupture, pregnancy and prior cesarean section, vaginal birth after cesarean, VBAC, trial of labor (TOL), trial of labor after cesarean (TOLAC), uterine scar dehiscence, and pregnancy and myomectomy as search terms; references were also traced. Eligible publications appeared from 1976 through May, 2012, reported rupture incidence, and provided enough information about their definitions of rupture and scar dehiscence. All included publications were observational studies or reviews; 133 articles underwent data extraction and analysis.

document_sections.heading: Incidence and risk factors
document_sections.content: A pooled analysis of 25 studies published from 1976-2012 gave an overall pregnancy-related rupture frequency of 1 per 1,416 pregnancies (0.07%). In 8 studies specifically describing spontaneous rupture of unscarred uteri in developed countries, it was 1 per 8,434 pregnancies (0.012%). Risk increases with congenital uterine anomalies, multiparity, previous myomectomy, the number and type of prior cesarean deliveries, fetal macrosomia, labor induction, uterine instrumentation, and trauma. Prior successful vaginal delivery and a longer interval after cesarean delivery may offer relative protection. Unlike models for predicting vaginal delivery after TOLAC, accurate individual rupture-risk prediction models are unavailable. Assessment considers whether the uterus is unscarred or has a cesarean or transabdominal or laparoscopic myomectomy scar; cesarean history includes single low transverse closure categorized by 1-layer or 2-layer closure, single low vertical, classic vertical, or multiple prior operations. Other considerations are congenital configuration, grand multiparity, maternal age, accreta, percreta, increta, previa, abruption, cornual or angular pregnancy, multiple gestation, polyhydramnios, macrosomia, contracted pelvis, gestation longer than 40 weeks, hydatidiform mole or choriocarcinoma with myometrial invasion, previous vaginal delivery, and interdelivery interval. Labor-related considerations include its absence, spontaneous onset, induction with oxytocin or prostaglandins, oxytocin augmentation, duration, and obstruction. Forceps, external cephalic version, internal podalic version, breech extraction, shoulder dystocia, manual placental extraction, fundal pressure, direct trauma, and violence are also listed. Table 1 presents absolute rupture rates by patient subgroup.

document_sections.heading: Rupture of the Unscarred Uterus
document_sections.content: A normal unscarred uterus has the lowest susceptibility. Grand multiparity, neglected labor, malpresentation, breech extraction, and uterine instrumentation predispose to rupture. In a 10-year Irish study, Gardeil et al found 1 rupture per 30,764 deliveries (0.0033%): none among 21,998 primigravidas and 2 (0.0051%) among 39,529 multigravidas without scars. An analysis of 8 large industrialized-country studies from 1975-2009 recorded 174 ruptures among 1,467,534 deliveries, suggesting an unscarred-uterus rate of 0.012% (1 in 8,434). This spontaneous rupture frequency has changed little over the last 50 years, and most cases arise at term during labor. In developing countries, the observed rate is 0.11% (1 in 920), an 8-fold increase attributed to more neglected and obstructed labor arising from inadequate medical access. The rates for unscarred uteri in industrialized and developing countries—0.012% (1 in 8,434) and 0.11% (1 in 920), respectively—serve as observational reference points when comparing risk groups.

document_sections.heading: Effect of maternal parity
document_sections.content: Many authors regard multiparity as a risk factor. Golan et al found parity greater than 5 in 19 of 61 rupture cases (31%); Schrinsky and Benson found parity greater than 4 in 7 of 22 women (32%) with unscarred-uterus rupture. Mokgokong and Marivate reported mean parity of 4 among women with pregnancy-related rupture. Despite the apparent excess risk with high parity, Gardeil et al observed only 2 ruptures among 39,529 multigravidas without a prior uterine scar (0.005%).

document_sections.heading: Rupture of the unscarred uterus before labor versus during labor
document_sections.content: Among 22 unscarred-uterus ruptures reported by Schrinsky and Benson, 19 occurred during labor (86%) and 3 before labor (14%). In contrast, antepartum and intrapartum rupture were distributed nearly equally among women with existing uterine scars.

document_sections.heading: Oxytocin augmentation and induction of labor in the unscarred uterus
document_sections.content: Oxytocin augmentation and induction involve patient groups with differing characteristics and typically differing doses, yet many rupture studies do not separate these uses. Mokgokong and Marivate reported 260 ruptures among 182,807 unscarred-uterus deliveries in 1976, with oxytocin use associated with 32 of the 260 (12%). Rahman et al reported oxytocin in 9 of 65 unscarred-uterus rupture cases (14%); Golan et al reported its use in 26 of 61 such cases (43%) among 126,713 deliveries. Plauche et al, however, attributed only 1 of 23 such ruptures (4%) to oxytocin. These limited findings leave the additional risk attributable to oxytocin in unscarred uteri uncertain. In women with previous cesarean delivery, oxytocin used for augmentation or induction appears associated with increased risk.

document_sections.heading: Congenital uterine anomalies
document_sections.content: Nahum's review estimated congenital uterine anomalies in approximately 1 in 200 women. With advancing pregnancy, affected uterine walls tend to become unusually thin, with thickness varying across the myometrium. During attempted VBAC, Ravasia et al observed rupture in 8% (2 of 25) of women with malformed uteri versus 0.61% (11 of 1,788) with normal uteri (P =.013); both anomaly-group ruptures followed induction with prostaglandin E2. Another study observed no rupture during spontaneous labor after 1 prior cesarean delivery in 165 patients with Müllerian duct anomalies. Of these, 36% (60 of 165) had minor arcuate or septate anomalies, 64% (105 of 165) had major unicornuate, didelphys, or bicornuate anomalies, and only 6% (10 of 165) underwent induction. For pregnancies implanted in a rudimentary uterine horn, induction is associated with particularly high rupture risk (≤ 81%; 387 of 475 cases); 80% of those ruptures occurred before the third trimester and 67% during the second trimester. Because rupture incidence is higher, induction decisions in congenital anomalies, particularly after cesarean delivery, require careful consideration. Although rupture risk in unscarred anomalous uteri exceeds that in normal uteri, the increase for each specific malformation remains uncertain.

document_sections.heading: Previous Uterine Myomectomy and Uterine Rupture
document_sections.content: The following sections distinguish outcomes after myomectomy by laparotomy from those after laparoscopic myomectomy.

document_sections.heading: Previous myomectomy by means of laparotomy
document_sections.content: Nearly all ruptures of uteri bearing myomectomy scars occur in the third trimester or labor; only 1 spontaneous rupture before 20 weeks of gestation has been reported. Brown et al observed no rupture among 120 term births after transabdominal myomectomy, with 80% delivered vaginally. Garnet instead identified 3 ruptures among 83 women (4%) with earlier myomectomy scars who underwent elective cesarean delivery because of that history. Reports often omit factors important for evaluating subsequent risk, including leiomyoma number, size, and site; uterine incision number and site; entry into the uterine cavity; and closure method. Further study is needed.

document_sections.heading: Previous laparoscopic myomectomy
document_sections.content: Dubuisson et al reported 3 subsequent pregnancy ruptures among 100 patients after laparoscopic myomectomy. Only 1 occurred at the prior scar, yielding an attributed rupture risk of 1% (95% CI, 0-5.5%). Whether the other 2 ruptures, which arose elsewhere, were caused by the earlier procedures is uncertain; if they were, the associated rate would instead be 3%. Four other studies found no pregnancy-related rupture among 320 pregnancies after laparoscopic myomectomy, but few patients were permitted to labor and scheduled cesarean delivery rates were 80%, 79%, 75%, and 65%, respectively. A prospective Japanese study found no rupture among 59 patients with successful vaginal birth after the procedure. An Italian multicenter study recorded 1 spontaneous rupture at 33 weeks' gestation among 386 patients who conceived after laparoscopic myomectomy (rupture rate 0.26%). Rupture has been reported as late as 8 years after the operation, indicating a need for additional long-term research.

document_sections.heading: Rupture of the Scarred Uterus Due to Previous Cesarean Delivery
document_sections.content: Previous cesarean delivery and rupture risk have been studied extensively. In a pooled analysis of 11 studies, Mozurkewich and Hutton reported rupture in 0.39% undergoing TOLAC versus 0.16% undergoing elective repeat cesarean delivery (odds ratio [OR], 2.10; 95% CI, 1.45-3.05). Restriction to 5 prospective cohort trials produced similar results (OR, 2.06; 95% CI, 1.40-3.04). Among 1,324 TOLAC patients, Hibbard et al found significantly different rupture frequencies after successful versus failed vaginal birth attempts (0.22% vs 1.9%; OR, 8.9; 95% CI, 1.9-42). Table 1 further divides rupture rates by cesarean-related characteristics. In the United States, VBAC rates rose from 3.4% in 1980 to 28% in 1996, alongside an 8-fold rise and increased reports of maternal and perinatal morbidity, particularly rupture. By 2007, VBAC had fallen to 8.5% while cesarean delivery reached 32%; VBAC then rose from 12.4% in 2016 to 12.8% in 2017 and 13.3% in 2018. Following a March 2010 NIH evidence review of VBAC maternal and neonatal outcomes, the most recent ACOG guidelines discussed here recommend against restricting access to VBAC. A multicountry population-based study reported rupture prevalence of 3.3 per 10,000 deliveries overall, 22 per 10,000 after previous cesarean section, and 0.6 per 10,000 without previous cesarean section. Countries combining low previous-cesarean rates with high TOLAC rates had more complete ruptures per TOLAC.

document_sections.heading: Previous classic cesarean delivery
document_sections.content: Classic cesarean delivery uses a vertical midline uterine incision, is now uncommon, and accounts for 0.5% of all United States births. Rosen et al's meta-analysis found rupture in 3 of 26 women (11.5%) with classic vertical scars undergoing unplanned TOLAC. Chauhan et al reported rupture in 0.64% of 157 women with such scars undergoing repeat cesarean delivery (95% CI, 0.13.5%); because preterm labor was frequent, 49% were in labor at surgery. Landon et al found rupture in 2 of 105 women (1.9%) with previous classic, inverted T, or J incisions who presented in advanced labor or declined repeat cesarean delivery. These frank-rupture rates contrast with the 4-9% historically reported by ACOG for these scars. Chauhan et al also observed asymptomatic scar dehiscence in 9% (95% CI, 5-15%), suggesting that earlier classification of dehiscence as rupture may explain much of the difference.

document_sections.heading: Previous low vertical cesarean delivery
document_sections.content: Across 5 pooled studies, symptomatic rupture affected 12 of 1,112 women (1.1%) undertaking TOLAC after a low vertical cesarean incision. Compared with low transverse scars, these findings suggest no significant increase in rupture or adverse maternal and perinatal outcomes. Interpretation is limited by inconsistent definitions of when a vertical incision extending upward becomes classic; even with a developed lower segment during active labor, a sufficiently long low vertical incision may not permit delivery. Naef et al arbitrarily classified extension of 2-cm into the upper segment as classic. Among 322 subsequent pregnancies after low vertical cesarean delivery, rupture occurred in 0.62% overall: 1.15% among 174 TOLAC patients and none among 148 receiving elective repeat cesarean delivery.

document_sections.heading: Unknown uterine scar
document_sections.content: When an earlier operative report is unavailable, obstetric history may help infer incision type: cesarean delivery at 28 weeks’ gestation is more likely to have involved a vertical incision than cesarean delivery for arrested fetal descent at term. The argument that an unknown scar carries the same risk as a low-transverse scar because most United States cesareans use low-transverse incisions neglects differences in indication, setting, medical resources, and local practice, including practices outside the United States such as in Mexico or Brazil. Nevertheless, the vast majority of United States cesarean incisions are low transverse. Leung et al's small case-control study of 70 patients found no association between unknown scar type and rupture, but was vastly underpowered because rupture is rare. Two similarly underpowered case series reported comparable rupture and VBAC-success rates for unknown scars and documented low-transverse incisions. The MFMU registry reported rupture in 0.5% (15 of 3,206) undertaking TOLAC with an unknown scar. In Grubb et al's small randomized trial among women with 1 or 2 unknown prior incisions, oxytocin augmentation (n=95) was compared with no intervention (n=93). Four dehiscences and 1 rupture occurred, all with augmentation. The rupture patient had 2 prior cesareans, including a vertical incision; knowledge of that incision would have constituted a contraindication to TOLAC.

document_sections.heading: Previous low transverse cesarean delivery
document_sections.content: Rupture risk after a low transverse cesarean varies with TOLAC versus elective repeat cesarean, induced versus spontaneous labor, and other factors. Most United States cesarean deliveries involve a low transverse incision. The ensuing sections and Table 1 describe absolute risks and contributing factors, particularly after 1 previous cesarean.

document_sections.heading: Previous cesarean delivery without a subsequent trial of labor
document_sections.content: In Lydon-Rochelle et al's study of 20,095 women, spontaneous rupture occurred in 0.16% of 6,980 women with a single cesarean scar who underwent scheduled repeat cesarean delivery without TOL. The authors interpret this as an intrinsic propensity for scarred uteri to rupture, exceeding the 0.012% risk in unscarred pregnancy by an OR increase of approximately 12-fold. They propose this expected rate as the comparison baseline for other groups with previous cesarean delivery.

document_sections.heading: Previous cesarean delivery with subsequent spontaneous labor
document_sections.content: Lydon-Rochelle et al observed rupture in 0.52% of 10,789 women who labored spontaneously in a subsequent singleton pregnancy after a single cesarean, corresponding to RR 3.3 (95% CI, 1.8-6.0) relative to elective repeat cesarean delivery. Ravasia et al reported 0.45% among 1,544 such patients, and Zelop et al reported 0.72% among 2,214. The article's meta-analysis of 29,263 pregnancies from 9 studies dating from 1987-2004 estimated 0.44% for spontaneous labor after cesarean.

document_sections.heading: Previous cesarean delivery with subsequent augmentation of labor
document_sections.content: Few studies separate augmentation from induction despite differences in patient characteristics and VBAC success; available findings conflict. Oxytocin use, dose, and schedules vary widely, leaving few specific evidence-based guidelines for its use during VBAC trials. Blanchette et al reported rupture in 1.4% of 288 women receiving oxytocin augmentation after cesarean versus 0.34% of 292 entering spontaneous labor, suggesting a 4fold increase. The MFMU Network reported 0.9% (52 of 6,009 cases) with augmentation versus 0.4% (24 of 6,685 cases) without oxytocin. Conversely, a meta-analysis of pre-1989 studies found no association, and Zelop et al found no significant augmentation-related increase. The pooled Table 1 results suggest a small upward trend, but their interpretation is limited and suspect because observational comparisons generally lack appropriate adjustment for likely confounding by indication, including proper propensity-score matching. Dose and exposure time both matter when evaluating oxytocin safety. In Cahill et al's nested case-control study of 804 patients within a retrospective multicenter cohort of 25,005 TOLAC patients with at least 1 prior cesarean, intravenous doses of 6-20 mU/min were associated with more than 3-fold higher rupture risk (HR [hazard ratio], 3.34, 95% CI 1.01-10.98); doses of more than 20 mU/min were associated with nearly 4-fold higher risk (HR, 3.92; 95% CI, 1.06-14.52). Attributable risks were 2.9% and 3.6% at maximum dose ranges of more than 20 mU/min and more than 30 mU/min, respectively. The investigators found no significant association for either duration of oxytocin exposure or labor duration. They suggested an upper oxytocin limit of 20 mU/min during VBAC trials and careful use and monitoring during augmentation or induction. The benefit of intrauterine pressure catheter (IUPC) monitoring remains unclear: a single small series found no fetal or maternal morbidity or mortality difference versus external tocodynamometry. Nevertheless, many institutions find IUPC useful for careful oxytocin titration when maternal habitus limits external contraction monitoring during TOLAC.

document_sections.heading: Previous cesarean delivery with subsequent induction of labor
document_sections.content: Emerging evidence suggests that induction after cesarean increases rupture risk. Zelop et al observed 2.3% among 560 induced patients versus 0.72% among 2,214 with spontaneous labor (P =.001). Ravasia et al found 1.4% among 575 induced patients versus 0.45% with spontaneous labor (P =.004). Blanchette et al found 4% after induction versus 0.34% after spontaneous labor, suggesting a 12-fold increase. Evidence on mechanical cervical ripening is limited but reassuring: Bujold et al's small series found rupture rates of 1.1% with spontaneous labor, 1.2% with amniotomy induction with or without oxytocin, and 1.6% with transcervical Foley catheter induction, without a significant difference (P =0.81). Conversely, Hoffman et al reported 3.67-fold greater risk with Foley catheter ripening (95% CI, 1.46-9.23), although many patients also received oxytocin. Pettker et al's randomized trial found that adding oxytocin to a transcervical Foley catheter neither shortened delivery time nor changed delivery within 24 hours or vaginal-delivery frequency. Foley catheter induction alone may therefore be reasonable for TOLAC with an unfavorable cervix. In a systematic review, Rossi and Prefumo compared induced labor (4,038 women) with spontaneous labor (13,374 women) after cesarean: induction had fewer vaginal births and more rupture/dehiscence, repeat cesareans, and postpartum hemorrhage, while hysterectomy and neonatal outcomes were similar. Facchinetti et al reported greater induction success with premature rupture of membranes and a favorable Bishop. Significant vaginal-delivery indicators were previous vaginal delivery, not being African, and induction for premature rupture of membranes. Repeat-cesarean patients more often had large infants (≥ 4 kg) and were more likely to have unsuccessful induction.

document_sections.heading: Use of prostaglandins for cervical ripening and induction of labor after previous cesarean delivery
document_sections.content: Current ACOG guidelines discourage prostaglandin induction in most women with previous cesarean delivery because substantial evidence links it to increased rupture risk. Lydon-Rochelle et al reported 15.6-fold greater risk (95% CI, 8.1-30) with prostaglandins during TOLAC; among 366 previously scarred women induced with these agents, rupture occurred in 2.45% versus 0.77% without them. Taylor et al recorded 3 ruptures among 58 women with 1 prior cesarean receiving prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) alone: 5.2% (3 of 58) versus 1.1% (8 of 732) without prostaglandin. Ravasia et al reported 1.7% (3 of 172) after induction with PGE2 alone, significantly above 0.45% (7 of 1,544) with spontaneous labor. In contrast, Flamm et al reported 1.3% (6 of 453) with PGE2 plus oxytocin versus 0.7% (33 of 4,569) without PGE2, a nonsignificant difference. Delaney and Young likewise found no significant difference between PGE2 induction and spontaneous labor after cesarean (1.1 vs 0.3%; P =.15). Landon et al observed no rupture among 227 patients induced with prostaglandins alone. Their study lacked power to identify small differences, and agent type appeared not to significantly alter risk; 52 received misoprostol, 111 dinoprostone, 60 PGE2 gel, and 4 combined prostaglandins.

document_sections.heading: Previous cesarean delivery with previous successful vaginal delivery
document_sections.content: Several studies associate prior vaginal birth with lower rupture risk during later attempts at vaginal birth after cesarean. Zelop et al compared 1,021 women with 1 previous vaginal delivery against 2,762 without one during TOL after a single cesarean: rates were 0.2% versus 1.1% (P =.01). Among women with a single scar, at least 1 earlier vaginal birth was associated with one fifth the risk (OR, 0.2; 95% CI, 0.04-0.8). Caughey et al reported approximately one fourth the risk with prior vaginal delivery (OR, 0.26; 95% CI, 0.08-0.88). Kayani and Alfirevic observed that all 4 ruptures among 205 TOL patients after 1 cesarean occurred in those without previous vaginal delivery. In an MFMU Network study of 11,778 women, induction versus spontaneous TOLAC significantly increased rupture among those without previous vaginal delivery (1.5% vs 0.8%, P =0.02); among those with prior vaginal birth, the spontaneous-versus-induced comparison was not significant (0.6% vs 0.4%, P =0.42).

document_sections.heading: Previous cesarean delivery with subsequent successful VBACs
document_sections.content: Multiple studies suggest prior successful VBAC lowers later rupture risk. Possible explanations offered are demonstration that the maternal bony pelvis permits fetal passage and that the scar previously tolerated labor and vaginal delivery without rupture. Mercer et al reported a decrease after the first successful VBAC but no demonstrated additional protection thereafter: 0.87% with no previous VBACs, 0.45% with one, and 0.43% with 2 or more (P =.01). Pooled results from 5 studies give a rupture rate of 1.4% (1 per 73) for failed VBAC attempts requiring repeat cesarean delivery during labor.

document_sections.heading: Interdelivery interval
document_sections.content: Esposito et al's case-control study found an interpregnancy interval of < 6 months nearly 4 times as frequent in rupture cases as controls (17.4 vs 4.7%; OR, 3.92; 95% CI, 1.0914.3). Among 23 patients with rupture after cesarean, the mean interval was 20.4 ± 15.4 months versus 36.5 ± 30.4 months in controls (P =.01). Stamilio et al reported rupture rates of 2.7% with an interdelivery interval of < 6 months versus 0.9% with ≥6 months (adjusted OR 2.66, 95% CI, 1.21-5.82). Shipp et al found 3-fold greater symptomatic rupture risk during TOLAC after 1 cesarean when the interval was < 18 months (OR, 3.0; 95% CI, 1.2-7.2), controlling for maternal age, public assistance, labor duration, gestational age of ³41 weeks, and induction or augmentation with oxytocin. Among 1,527 women undertaking TOL after a single low-transverse cesarean, Bujold et al found rupture in 2.8% with an interval of ≤24 months versus 0.9% with >24 months (P< .01); the adjusted odds ratio was 2.65 (95% CI, 1.08-5.46). Their follow-up analysis found a significant increase with an interval shorter than 18 months (odds ratio [OR], 3; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.3–7.2), but not with 18-24 months (OR, 1.1; 95% CI, 0.4–3.2); they regarded only the shorter interval as a risk factor. The authors speculated that longer intervals permit scar tensile strength to mature before another pregnancy. They also found rupture in 5.6% when an interval of ≤24 months coincided with single-layer hysterotomy closure, comparable to the rate with a prior classic midline scar during TOLAC.

document_sections.heading: One-layer versus 2-layer hysterotomy closure
document_sections.content: In a Canadian study of 1,980 TOL patients after one low transverse cesarean, Bujold et al found a 4to 5-fold greater rupture risk after single-layer than two-layer closure: 3.1% (15 of 489 cases) versus 0.5% (8 of 1,491 cases; P< .001). Stepwise multivariate logistic regression yielded OR 3.95 (95% CI, 1.35-11.49) for single-layer versus two-layer closure. The same authors' multicenter case-control study compared 96 rupture cases with 288 controls and found more than twice the risk after single-layer closure (multivariate odds ratio [OR] 2.69; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.37–5.28); they concluded that women contemplating later VBAC should avoid single-layer closure. Durnwald and Mercer found no increased rupture rate among 182 single-layer-closure patients, but uterine windows at the next delivery were more frequent than after multilayer closure (3.5% versus 0.7%; P =.046). Gyamfi et al reported rupture in 8.6% (3 of 35) after single-layer versus 1.3% (12 of 913) after double-layer closure (P =0.015). Despite a shorter interdelivery interval in the single-layer group, adjustment retained a significant difference (OR 7.20, 95% CI, 1.81-28.62, P =0.005).

document_sections.heading: Multiple prior cesarean deliveries
document_sections.content: Across 10 studies published from 1993-2010, rupture after 2 or more cesareans ranged from 0.9-6.0% (1 per 17-108 pregnancies), a 2- to 16-fold increase relative to a single prior cesarean. Miller et al studied 17,322 women with cesarean scars and found rupture during TOLAC 3 times more often with 2 or more scars than with 1 (1.7% versus 0.6%; OR, 3.06; 95% CI, 1.95-4.79; P< .001). In data from 17 hospitals, Macones et al found twice the risk among 1,082 TOLAC patients with 2 scars versus 1 (1.8% vs 0.9%; adjusted OR, 2.3; 95% CI, 1.37-3.85). Caughey et al's study, described as the only one controlling potential confounders, found almost 5 times the risk after 2 versus 1 prior cesarean during attempted vaginal delivery (3.7% vs 0.8%; P =.001). Controlled variables included prostaglandin E2 gel, oxytocin induction and augmentation, labor length, and epidural use; prior vaginal delivery was associated with approximately one fourth the risk (OR, 0.26; 95% CI, 0.08-0.88). In contrast, Landon et al's MFMU Network analysis found no significant difference for multiple versus 1 previous cesarean (0.9% vs 0.7%; P= 0.37). Their multiple-cesarean TOLAC rate was 9%, versus 27% in Macones et al and 73% in Miller et al, suggesting stricter selection could explain discrepant results. Caughey et al did not give a TOLAC rate for their 12-year analysis. A meta-analysis of 17 studies including 5,666 women attempting TOL after 2 or more cesareans found rupture in 1.36%. The article's pooled analysis of 10 studies from 1993-2010 found 1.81% with multiple scars. A 2004 ACOG guideline suggested considering TOLAC after 2 cesareans only with previous vaginal delivery; its revised 2010 guideline suggested women with two prior low transverse cesareans may be considered regardless of previous vaginal-delivery history.

document_sections.heading: Previous complete uterine rupture
document_sections.content: Thisted et al reported recurrent rupture in 8.6% of pregnant women with previous complete rupture during TOLAC versus 0.8% of controls (OR, 11.7; 95% CI, 1.36-543.1). Previous complete rupture was also associated with significantly more miscarriage (OR, 3.99; 95% CI, 1.36-13.17). Fox's review included 37 women (59 pregnancies) with earlier rupture and 50 women (75 pregnancies) with earlier dehiscence; rupture occurred in one subsequent pregnancy (0.7% of pregnancies; 1.2% of women), with no deaths.

document_sections.heading: Maternal age
document_sections.content: Shipp et al associated increasing maternal age with higher rupture risk. Among 3,015 women with 1 earlier cesarean, overall rupture was 1.1%; rates were significantly different for women older than 30 years versus younger women (1.4% versus 0.5%; OR, 3.2; 95% CI, 1.2-8.4) in an analysis controlling confounders.

document_sections.heading: Multiple gestation
document_sections.content: Most large twin-VBAC series report rupture frequencies similar to singleton pregnancies. Ford et al found 0.9% among 1,850 twin-VBAC attempts versus 0.8% for singleton gestations using United States inpatient data from 1993-2002. Cahill et al compared 535 twin pregnancies with 24,307 singleton pregnancies during TOLAC after at least 1 cesarean and reported 1.1% versus 0.9% (OR, 1.2; 95% CI, 0.3-4.6). Twin patients were less likely to undertake TOLAC (OR, 0.3; 95% CI 0.2-.04), but were no more likely to experience VBAC failure (OR, 1.1; 95% CI, 0.8-1.6) or major maternal morbidity (OR, 1.6; 95% CI, 0.7-3.7). Overall, multifetal VBAC attempts did not show greater rupture risk than singleton controls. In a nested MFMU registry case-control study after one prior cesarean, Varner et al reported the same 0.7% frequency for multifetal (4/556) and singleton pregnancies (99/13,923) [ORadj 1.19 (0.43-3.30)]. Aaronson et al found no ruptures among 134 twin TOLAC pregnancies after a single cesarean. ACOG 2010 VBAC guidelines allow consideration of TOLAC for otherwise suitable twin-vaginal-delivery candidates with one previous low transverse cesarean.

document_sections.heading: Fetal macrosomia
document_sections.content: Elkousy et al studied 9,960 TOLAC patients after 1 cesarean and found significantly more rupture when fetal weight exceeded 4000 g than when it was below 4000 g (2.8% versus 1.2%; RR 2.3, P< .001). In those without prior vaginal delivery, rupture with fetal weight above 4000 g was 3.6% compared with fetal weight < 4000 g (RR 2.3, P< .001). Jastrow et al found rates increasing with birth weight: 0.9% below 3500 g, 1.8% at 3500-3999 g, and 2.6% at 4000 g or larger (P< .05). Zelop et al observed 1.6% for neonates >4000 g versus 1% for those ≤4000 g, without statistical significance (P =0.24). Flamm et al found no rupture-rate difference between ≥4000 gm and < 4000 gm among 301 TOLAC patients. ACOG 2010 VBAC guidelines suggest suspected macrosomia alone should not rule out TOLAC.

document_sections.heading: Gestation beyond 40 weeks
document_sections.content: Gestational age affects counseling about postterm TOLAC safety and success, but findings conflict. Hammoud et al's Canadian study found rupture in 2.7% of 329 women at ≥41 weeks versus 1.0% of 1,911 at 37-40 6/7 weeks (p=0.006). After adjustment, later gestation was associated with less successful vaginal delivery (OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.51–0.89) and more rupture (OR 2.85, 95% CI 1.27–6.42) relative to 37–40 6/7 weeks. Kiran et al's British study similarly found 2.1% (10 of 466) beyond 40 weeks versus 0.3% (4 of 1,154) at ≤40 weeks (OR6.3,CI1.9-20.2). The largest study, by Coassolo et al, did not find this association: at 40 weeks or longer, rupture occurred in 1.1% (52 of 4,680) versus 1.0% (68 of 6,907) before 40 weeks, without a significant difference; defining the later group as 41 weeks' gestation or longer also showed no increase in rupture or overall morbidity. Differences may reflect small Canadian and British samples and/or uncertainty about gestational dating with last menstrual period and early ultrasound confirmation in Coassalo et al. Zelop et al likewise found no significant difference: 1.3% (17 of 1,271) beyond 40 weeks versus 0.8% (12 of 1,504) at 37-40 weeks (P = 0.2). Those authors concluded that rupture does not rise substantially solely after 40 weeks but does increase with induction regardless of gestational age. With spontaneous labor, rates were 0.5% at or before 40 weeks versus 1.0% afterward (P = 0.2); with induced labor, they were 2.1% versus 2.6% (P = 0.7). ACOG 2010 VBAC guidance suggests that later gestation may lower vaginal-birth success but, alone, should not exclude TOLAC. Table 1 lists subgroup-specific absolute rupture rates.

document_sections.heading: Signs and Symptoms of Uterine Rupture During Pregnancy
document_sections.content: Clinical findings depend on when rupture occurs and on defect location and extent. Rupture through a previous scar is generally less dramatic than spontaneous or traumatic rupture because the scar is relatively less vascular. Classically described findings include fetal distress, usually reflected in fetal heart-rate abnormalities; reduced baseline uterine pressure; loss of contractility; abdominal pain; recession of the presenting fetal part; hemorrhage; and shock. Modern studies show that some are rare or difficult to distinguish from findings in less serious obstetric situations. Table 2 summarizes associated findings and their frequency. Prolonged, late, or recurrent variable fetal-heart-rate decelerations and bradycardia are often the earliest and sole clues. Bujold and Gauthier found an abnormal fetal-heart-rate pattern as the first manifestation in 87%; Leung et al observed prolonged decelerations in 79%, their most common associated finding; and Rodriguez et al reported fetal distress in 78%, also the most common finding. Across 4 studies from 1983-2000, prolonged deceleration or bradycardia occurred in 114 (80%) of 143 ruptures. Prolonged decelerations invariably accompanied fetal and placental extrusion into the abdomen. Abrupt or atypical maternal abdominal pain is less frequent than fetal deceleration or bradycardia: across 9 studies from 19802002 it occurred in 13-60% of ruptures. Among 10,967 TOLAC patients, only 22% of complete ruptures presented with pain, versus 76% with fetal distress on continuous electronic monitoring. Bujold and Gauthier found pain as the first manifestation in only 5%, occurring without epidural analgesia but not with an epidural block. Pain is therefore an uncommon, unreliable indicator. Concerns that epidural anesthesia conceals rupture pain have not been verified, and no diagnostic delay attributable to epidural anesthesia has been reported. ACOG's 2010 guideline suggests no absolute contraindication to epidural anesthesia during TOLAC, since it rarely masks rupture findings. Phelan et al found that uterine tetany and hyperstimulation often did not signal rupture; their externally monitored study defined tetany as a contraction longer than 90 seconds and hyperstimulation as more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes. Rodriguez et al found no support for IUPCs as a rupture diagnostic aid: none of 76 rupture patients showed the classically described decline in uterine tone or activity, including the 39 with IUPCs. Fetal and maternal morbidity and mortality after rupture were similar with IUPC and external monitoring. Across 8 reports from 1980-2002, vaginal bleeding occurred in 11-67% of rupture cases. Across 3 studies, hypovolemic maternal shock occurred in 29-46%.

document_sections.heading: Diagnosis
document_sections.content: Because irreversible fetal injury can develop quickly, prolonged diagnostic investigations and sophisticated imaging have limited usefulness; diagnosis is most appropriately based on standard clinical findings summarized in Table 2. Techniques have nevertheless been studied for individual risk assessment. Amniography, radiopelvimetry, and pelvic examination have proved unsuitable for predicting rupture in TOLAC candidates. CT and MRI are not clinically useful for acute diagnosis because of the time required, although MRI is considered better than CT for assessing an incision because it provides greater soft-tissue contrast. Studies of these approaches are limited by retrospective designs and lack of surgical verification of actual dehiscence. Reports suggest transabdominal or transvaginal ultrasound or sonohysterography may identify cesarean-scar defects. Rozenberg et al prospectively studied 642 women and found that rupture risk after cesarean rose as lower-uterine-segment thickness fell on transabdominal ultrasound at 36-38 weeks of gestation, increasing significantly below 3.5 mm. At a 3.5 mm cutoff, sensitivity was 88%, specificity 73.2%, positive predictive value 11.8%, and negative predictive value 99.3% for later rupture. Gotoh et al studied 722 women and reported significantly higher rupture risk with an ultrasound-measured uterine wall thinner than 2 mm within 1 week of delivery; positive and negative predictive values were 73.9% and 100%, respectively.

document_sections.heading: Consequences of Uterine Rupture
document_sections.content: The following sections address fetal and maternal consequences separately.

document_sections.heading: Overview
document_sections.content: Consequences depend on the time from rupture to definitive treatment. Fetal treatment is delivery, which must generally occur rapidly to avoid major morbidity and death. Maternal care can generally begin with support and resuscitation until surgery controls potentially life-threatening bleeding. Several studies indicate delivery within 10-37 minutes of rupture is needed to prevent serious fetal morbidity or mortality. With fluid resuscitation and blood transfusion available, the interval before definitive surgery causes major maternal harm can often be considerably longer than the corresponding fetal interval. Table 3 summarizes fetal and maternal consequences.

document_sections.heading: Fetal and Neonatal Consequences of Uterine Rupture
document_sections.content: Leung et al found neonatal asphyxia—umbilicalartery pH < 7 together with seizures and multiorgan dysfunction—in 5 of 99 newborns (5%) after maternal rupture. No clinically important perinatal morbidity occurred when delivery followed an isolated prolonged fetal-heart-rate deceleration within 17 minutes; when severe late decelerations preceded it, asphyxia appeared as early as 10 minutes from prolonged-deceleration onset to delivery. Menihan observed fetal bradycardia 18-37 minutes before delivery in 6 of 11 fetuses following rupture; fetal acidosis occurred in 91%, but there was no permanent neurologic injury or neonatal death. Among 23 ruptures, Bujold and Gauthier found that intervention in < 18-min after prolonged deceleration still left 2 neonates with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy and impaired motor development. They concluded prompt treatment probably reduced neonatal deaths but could not invariably avert severe metabolic acidosis or serious neonatal illness. Leung et al reported umbilical-artery pH below 7 in 43 of 99 newborns (43%), including 25 with pH below 6.8; 39 (39%) had 5-minute Apgar scores below 7, including 12 below 3. Menihan reported umbilical-artery pH below 7.0 in 10 of 11 fetuses (91%), and 5-minute Apgar scores below 7 in 5 (45%); complete fetal and placental extrusion into the maternal abdomen was the most important factor for acidosis. NICU admission after rupture was reported by Menihan in 8 of 11 newborns (73%), by Kieser and Baskett in 45% (8 of 18), and by Landon et al in 32% (46 of 144 newborns). Fetal mortality was high in studies before 1978: Schrinsky and Benson's review of 33 studies found 620 infant deaths among 960 ruptures, a perinatal mortality rate of 65%. Blanchette et al reported death of 2 neonates (17%) among 12 maternal rupture cases, including 1 after a decision-to-delivery interval of only 26 minutes following acute bradycardia, lower abdominal pain, and vaginal bleeding. Leung et al found 6 perinatal deaths (6%) among 99 rupture patients. Lydon-Rochelle et al reported perinatal death in 5.5% of fetuses from 91 rupture cases versus 0.5% in controls. Landon et al reported 2% (2 of 124) across 19 United States academic centers. Together, these reports indicate declining rupture-associated perinatal mortality in the modern era.

document_sections.heading: Maternal Consequences of Uterine Rupture
document_sections.content: Cowan et al reported mean blood loss of 1,500 mL in 5 rupture patients, symptomatic in 3 (60%). Transfusion after rupture was reported by Shipp et al in 25% (7 of 28 women) during TOLAC, Kieser and Baskett in 44% (8 of 18 patients) with complete rupture, and Leung et al in 29% (29 of 99). Hypovolemic shock occurred in 29% of 93 rupture patients in Golan et al and in 33 (34%) of 96 women in Rahman et al; these modern frequencies appear lower than Eden et al's 53-year literature review finding of 46% (11 of 24 cases). Lydon-Rochelle et al found important bladder injuries in 8% (7 of 91) of women with rupture versus 1.2% (240 of 20,004) without rupture (P =.001). Shipp et al reported bladder injury in 18% (5 of 28) after rupture following low transverse cesarean, and Kieser and Baskett reported cystotomy in 17% (3 of 18). Leung et al found incidental operative cystotomy in 12% (12 of 99) and ruptured bladder or accidental cystotomy in another 7 (7%), for 19% urologic injury overall. Hysterectomy was performed in 78% (261 of 335) of South African rupture patients, 8% (3 of 39) in Flamm et al, 6% (1 of 18) after complete rupture in Kieser and Baskett, 17% (2 of 12) in Blanchette et al, and 60% (6 of 10) in Hibbard et al. Leung et al reported hysterectomy in 19% (19 of 99): 13 (68%) because repair was judged impossible, 4 (21%) because of uncontrollable uterine atony, and 1 (5%) because of placenta accreta. Rupture-related maternal mortality is reported at 0-1% in modern developed nations versus 5-10% in developing countries; availability of modern facilities likely contributes to the difference. In a 1976 South African study, 22 of 260 women with rupture of an unscarred uterus died (8.5%). By tear type, deaths involved 15 of 183 patients [8.2%] with longitudinal tears, 2 of 49 patients [4%] with transverse tears, 2 of 16 patients [13%] with posterior-wall tears, and 3 of 12 patients [25%] with multiple tears. Golan et al found no deaths among 32 women with scarred-uterus rupture versus 9 deaths among 61 with an intact uterus (15%). Leung et al reported 1 death (1%) among 99 Los Angeles rupture patients. Mokgokong and Marivate reported maternal mortality of 4.5% when diagnosis preceded delivery versus 10.4% when it followed delivery.

document_sections.heading: Management of the Ruptured Uterus
document_sections.content: The following sections discuss urgent treatment and prevention strategies.

document_sections.heading: Treatment
document_sections.content: Timely recognition and a short interval between initial manifestations and definitive surgery are essential. Once rupture is diagnosed, immediate maternal stabilization and fetal delivery are imperative. After frank rupture, the interval before major fetal morbidity is generally only 10-37 minutes; when rupture is suspected, available resources should be mobilized rapidly for definitive surgical care. After delivery, maternal surgery is guided by rupture type and extent, bleeding severity, maternal condition, and wishes about future childbearing. Longitudinal tears generally bleed more heavily than transverse tears. Uterine repair as conservative surgical treatment should be reserved for women desiring future childbearing who have a low transverse rupture without extension into the broad ligament, cervix, or paracolpos; readily controlled bleeding; good general condition; and no clinical or laboratory evidence of developing coagulopathy. Hysterectomy should be considered the preferred treatment for uncontrollable uterine hemorrhage or multiple, longitudinal, or low-lying rupture sites. Clinicians should maintain strong suspicion, especially in high-risk patients, and act rapidly and decisively when uncertain.

document_sections.heading: Prevention
document_sections.content: Absolute pregnancy-related rupture risk is low but varies substantially by subgroup, as shown in Table 1. The lowest-risk group has a normal, unscarred uterus, with 1 in 8,434 pregnancies [0.012%]. The most direct proposed preventive approach is to reduce exposure of the highest-risk groups, although the acceptable-risk threshold is ultimately arbitrary and should reflect patients', physicians', and society's tolerance. At a threshold of 1 in 200 women (0.5%), groups above it include multiple prior cesareans; classic midline or low vertical cesarean scars; low transverse cesarean with single-layer closure; an interdelivery interval of less than 2 years after cesarean; a low transverse scar plus congenital uterine anomaly; previous cesarean without prior successful vaginal birth; induction or augmentation after cesarean; a prior cesarean with a fetus weighing >4000 g; and laparoscopic or laparotomy myomectomy. For patients in these categories, whose rupture risk exceeds 1 in 200, a management plan should explicitly account for that increased risk.

document_sections.heading: Conclusion
document_sections.content: Rupture is uncommon but often catastrophic; the stated overall incidence is approximately 1 in 1,536 pregnancies (0.07%). For normal, unscarred uteri in modern industrialized countries, it is 1 in 8,434 pregnancies (0.012%). Most ruptures occur in scarred uteri, predominantly after cesarean delivery. The stated overall rate rises to 0.5% with a single cesarean scar and 2% with 2 or more. Additional higher-risk groups include single-layer hysterotomy closure, a short interval after cesarean, congenital anomaly, macrosomic fetus, prostaglandin exposure, and an unsuccessful previous vaginal-delivery trial. Surgery in less than 10-37 minutes after rupture is essential to reduce permanent fetal injury, although delivery within that interval cannot always prevent severe fetal hypoxia, metabolic acidosis, or serious neonatal consequences. Prolonged, persistent, profound fetal bradycardia is the most consistent early indicator; abdominal pain, abnormal labor progress, and vaginal bleeding are less dependable diagnostically. A general goal of starting cesarean delivery within 20-30 minutes after diagnosing fetal distress has minimal usefulness in rupture: fetal or placental extrusion can cause irreversible fetal injury earlier. Acting within that interval may nevertheless help prevent maternal exsanguination and death if supportive and resuscitative care is available before definitive surgery.
